analysis.one_liner: Requires the federal government and its contractors to pay workers a wage above the poverty line.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended, dying in committee with 20 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the federal government and every employer holding a federal contract over $10,000 to pay each worker at least the federal poverty level for a family of four, calculated as a full-time hourly wage, plus a locality-based top-up to cover fringe benefits like health care and retirement contributions the employer does not provide. Employers that repeatedly violated the wage rule could lose their federal contracts and be barred from federal contracting for five years, and workers could sue for back pay and triple damages for willful violations. Small businesses and certain nonprofits with modest pay gaps between executives and lowest-paid workers were exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers employed by the federal government or by federal contractors, particularly low-wage service and subcontracting workers who currently earn under the poverty line, would gain a guaranteed wage floor tied to the cost of supporting a family. Their families would also gain access to employer-paid health, retirement, and other benefits or the cash equivalent, and the anti-retaliation and lawsuit provisions give them a way to enforce it.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the federal government and employers on federal contracts over $10,000 to pay workers at least the federal poverty level for a family of four on a full-time schedule, with an added locality-based amount to cover any fringe benefits not provided.

Makes contractors with a pattern of wage violations subject to contract cancellation, restitution of the government's replacement costs, a five-year federal contracting ban, and public notice in the Federal Register.

Prohibits employers from firing or suspending workers who allege a wage violation, and lets aggrieved workers sue for injunctions, actual damages (triple damages for willful violations), attorney fees, and costs.
Exempts small businesses and tax-exempt nonprofits whose chief executive earns no more than 25 times their lowest-paid worker, and allows the President to suspend the requirements during emergencies.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors and subcontractors over $10,000, and the federal government itself as an employer, would bear higher labor costs, which large service and support contractors would likely pass through to the government in contract bids, meaning some of the cost would land on federal taxpayers. Nonprofit and small-business employers were carved out.

drawbacks.text: Higher wages would raise federal procurement costs, and contractors could pass much of the increase to taxpayers through higher bids on the next contract cycle.

The bill's definition of 'employer' — anyone with the economic power to set a worker's terms — reaches beyond traditional employers and could create compliance disputes, and the executive-to-worker pay-ratio test for nonprofits would be a novel rule to administer.

The exemptions for small businesses and for nonprofits with a 25-to-1 executive pay ratio leave many low-wage employers unaffected, so the wage floor would be uneven across the federal contractor workforce.
The Secretary's safe harbor lets a contractor avoid cancellation or debarment by settling with the government and paying back wages, which could soften the enforcement teeth in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and measurable: a full-time worker on a federal contract could no longer be paid below the poverty line for a family of four, with enforcement through debarment and private lawsuits. The main real cost is higher federal procurement spending, part of which would flow back to the workers and part to contractors' margins; part of the benefit could also be captured by contractors who pass costs through. The design is roughly workable, with some loose edges in the employer definition and the nonprofit pay-ratio test, but the bill's practical impact was never tested because it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2006 and sent to two House committees, then referred to a subcommittee on workforce protections, and no committee ever voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the Federal Living Wage Responsibility Act on July 28, 2006, with 19 Democratic colleagues and one Independent joining as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Government Reform Committee and the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced.
On September 28, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a Senate counterpart in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors and other employers of low-wage federal workers were better off, since their labor costs were never raised; the bill's cosponsors and low-wage workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal contractors who avoided higher labor costs

for.name: Rep. Luis V. Gutierrez

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Reps. Nadler, Cummings, McGovern, Schakowsky, Baldwin, Lantos, and Tierney.

against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over labor standards

against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over federal contracting
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after its referral; no committee action appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led House committees never acted on it.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and subcontractors (services, support, and labor-intensive firms)
industries.note: These firms would have to pay every worker at least the poverty-level wage for a family of four plus benefit top-ups, raising labor costs on contracts over $10,000; repeated violators would face contract cancellation and a five-year contracting ban. Their cost savings from low wages are exactly what the bill targeted, and low-wage federal contract workers stood on the other side of that trade.

industries.industry: Defense and procurement firms relying on low-wage subcontract labor
industries.note: The wage mandate and debarment penalty would raise costs and compliance risk on large contracts, but costs could partly be passed to the government in future bids, shifting the burden to taxpayers.
The bill exempts small business concerns, giving them a cost advantage over large contractors that would have to pay the wage floor on the same government work.
Nonprofits are exempt only if their CEO earns no more than 25 times their lowest-paid worker, so the bill would have used pay-ratio compliance as a condition of the wage mandate for this sector.
